questions.q: Name the causative agents of gonorrhoea, syphilis, and chlamydiasis, and state one common symptom shared by all three.
questions.a: Gonorrhoea: Neisseria gonorrhoeae (bacterium); Syphilis: Treponema pallidum (spirochaete bacterium); Chlamydiasis: Chlamydia trachomatis (obligate intracellular bacterium). Common symptom: mucopurulent urethral/vaginal discharge (often asymptomatic in women). A wrong answer (e.g., naming viruses or fungi) reveals confusion between bacterial and viral STDs; missing the shared symptom indicates failure to recognise that bacterial STDs often present with similar inflammatory discharge.

questions.q: Why is the "ABC" strategy (Abstinence, Be faithful, Condoms) more effective against bacterial STDs than against viral STDs like HIV or HPV?
questions.a: ABC reduces exposure to infected fluids/skin, which prevents bacterial transmission effectively because bacteria require direct mucosal contact and do not integrate into host genome. Viral STDs like HIV can also transmit via blood, mother-to-child, or needle-sharing — routes not addressed by ABC alone; HPV spreads through skin-to-skin contact in areas not covered by condoms. A wrong answer (e.g., "condoms block all viruses equally") shows misunderstanding of transmission modes and condom limitations.

questions.q: A 24-year-old woman presents with frothy, yellow-green vaginal discharge, vulval itching, and a "strawberry cervix" on examination. Identify the STD, its causative agent, and the drug of choice.
questions.a: STD: Trichomoniasis; Causative agent: Trichomonas vaginalis (flagellated protozoan); Drug of choice: Metronidazole (single 2 g oral dose). Steps: (1) Frothy yellow-green discharge + strawberry cervix = classic trichomoniasis. (2) Protozoan STDs are treated with nitroimidazoles, not antibiotics. (3) Partner must be treated simultaneously to prevent reinfection. A wrong answer (e.g., "Candida, treated with fluconazole") confuses protozoal with fungal infection; missing partner treatment reveals ignorance of reinfection cycles.

questions.q: Compare the long-term complications of untreated syphilis and untreated HPV infection in women. Which poses a greater risk of malignancy?
questions.a: Untreated syphilis progresses through primary (chancre), secondary (rash, condylomata lata), latent, and tertiary stages (gummas, cardiovascular/neurosyphilis) — rarely malignant. Untreated high-risk HPV (types 16, 18) persists and integrates into host DNA, causing cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) → cervical cancer. HPV poses far greater malignancy risk. A wrong answer (e.g., "syphilis causes cancer") confuses chronic inflammation with oncogenic viral integration; missing CIN progression shows gap in viral carcinogenesis knowledge.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "Vaccination alone can eliminate STDs from a population." Support your judgement with two biological reasons.
questions.a: False. (1) Vaccines exist only for Hepatitis B and HPV — not for bacterial (gonorrhoea, syphilis, chlamydia), protozoal (trichomoniasis), or other viral STDs (HIV, HSV). (2) Vaccines prevent infection but do not treat existing infections; asymptomatic carriers continue transmission. Elimination requires combined biomedical (vaccines, treatment), behavioural (ABC), and structural (screening, partner notification) interventions. A wrong answer (e.g., "true, vaccines give herd immunity") ignores the limited vaccine portfolio and the role of asymptomatic reservoirs.

questions.q: Design a community-level intervention to reduce STD incidence among migrant workers in an industrial town. Include one behavioural, one biomedical, and one structural component.
questions.a: Behavioural: Peer-led workshops in native language promoting condom use and reducing stigma. Biomedical: Monthly mobile clinic offering free syndromic management (WHO flowcharts) + Hepatitis B/HPV vaccination camps. Structural: Employer-mandated paid leave for STD treatment + confidential partner-notification slips. Good answer integrates all three levels; poor answer focuses only on condoms or only on clinics, missing the socio-ecological model.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Sexually Transmitted Diseases (STDs) are infections transmitted primarily through unprotected sexual contact (vaginal, anal, or oral) caused by bacteria, viruses, protozoa, or fungi; they affect the reproductive tract and can lead to serious ______ like infertility, cancer, or systemic illness if untreated.
Fill in the blank: Imagine a 19-year-old college student in Delhi who notices a painless ulcer on the genitals after ______ sex — this could be the primary chancre of syphilis, a bacterial STD.
What is Sexually Transmitted Diseases (STDs)? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Sexually Transmitted Diseases (STDs) are infections transmitted primarily through unprotected sexual contact (vaginal, anal, or oral) caused by bacteria, viruses, protozoa, or fungi; they affect the reproductive tract and can lead to serious complications like infertility, cancer, or systemic illness if untreated.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Sexually Transmitted Diseases (STDs)?
questions.a: Students think "STD = HIV" and believe all STDs are viral, incurable, and always symptomatic.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can classify at least 6 major STDs by causative agent (bacterial/viral/protozoal/fungal), describe two key symptoms for each, explain the ABC prevention strategy, and justify why early detection and partner notification break transmission chains.
